ingredients.item: of dried roasted seaweed , the plain unseasoned kind

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: The dressing whisked smooth — soy, water, honey, garlic — in the bowl that will hold the finished banchan.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the dressing tastes like a strong dip: salty, sweet, sharp — the seaweed's mineral dryness will demand exactly this strength.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: The ribbons in, tossed gently with your hands (tongs shred; hands coat) until every ribbon goes from dry-crisp to glossy-supple, then sesame oil and seeds worked through.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the transformation is the checkpoint: the ribbons soften and darken into glistening strands that hold together on a spoon, no crispness left. Work fast and stop at uniformly glossy — over-tossed seaweed breaks down to flakes.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Scallion and gochugaru over, and the bowl is served within the hour.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test with rice: a soft, savory, mineral-deep tangle — the sea's version of the spinach bowl (#B06), and the same reset-the-palate job. If it tastes only of the dressing, the seaweed was weak or old (seaweed that has lost its sea-smell has lost its reason).

storageNotes: Same-day only (see Note — the tradition's own rule). The dry sheets keep a year sealed; the bowl never keeps.
Variations: the gochugaru-forward fork for color and warmth; julienned cucumber folded through for crunch; the same dressing over torn fresh wakame runs at the soft end of the family.
